glossary.meaning: When the persecutor came, some clergy handed the scriptures over to be burned. We called such a man a traditor. We held that his hand was no longer clean, and that he could not ordain, baptize, or bless. What flowed from that hand was nothing at all.

We did not think of this as baptizing twice. Nothing happened the first time. A hand from a tainted line washes nothing. So when someone came to us from the other church, we gave the first real baptism they had had.

A martyr dies for the true faith. But our best-known dead were not killed by pagans. They were killed by imperial troops sent at the urging of a rival Christian party. That party did not grant them the word. We did not accept its account of our own dead.

There was no neutral word for the church here. The word itself was the argument. Two whole rival bodies claimed it, town by town, bishop for bishop. We held that we were the true one, and that our rival's favour with the state settled nothing.

We held that the state had no standing to say which church was the true one. 'What has the Emperor to do with the Church?' -- so our primate is reported to have asked. Yet three times we went to that same court when it served us. We held both facts at once, and called neither one a lie.
glossary.world_word: Quid est imperatori cum ecclesia? ("What has the emperor to do with the church?")

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Anonymous inscribers of this communion, on two pillars near Bagai (CIL VIII 17732), with three further stones carrying the same words

pull_quotes.text: What business does the emperor have with the church?
Truth is hidden by a great device: when we ask, the other side puts forward a small part, and the rest is kept silent.

What we look for is the conscience of the giver, the one who gives in holiness, to cleanse the conscience of the one who receives. For whoever knowingly takes faith from the faithless does not receive faith, but guilt.

cite.text:
If you came to us from the other communion, we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way." Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Wrong done to us, and whether the wrongdoer could come back, got three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And Tyconius, who would not stop preaching a doctrine his bishop forbade, is reported to have been condemned by a council of his own communion, and he was never received back at all. So a wrongdoer could come back to us. It depended on who the wrongdoer was. No rule of ours survives that explains the difference. The one reason we know comes from a writer named Cresconius. His own book is lost. His reason reaches us only through Augustine's answer to him.

On prayer, the meal and fasting, what we can show thins out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed with their hands stretched out to the Lord and their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a woman was said to have kissed a martyr's bone before she took it, and was rebuked for it. We know one man, held four days before he was thrown from a cliff, ended his last day with a fast. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last days. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: How did a person actually become one of you? Walk me through it.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Everyone who came to us from the rival church crossed through one act, the washing. It was no hurdle to clear before belonging, and no repeat of something already valid. We held that a hand which gave up the scriptures to be burned could not afterward be trusted to give what it claimed to give. So no washing that came from such a hand had ever been a baptism at all, however much it looked like one. What happened at our own font was the first true entry into the body whose Lord it actually is. It was dated. It was remembered. It marked, plainly, who was truly among us.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: That's the doctrine. But tell me about your baptism -- what was it like?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We did not set one man's day apart from every other. What we can give you is what everyone crossing to us had crossed through, the same each time it was done: the washing, which we counted as the first true baptism, because no washing given by an untrustworthy hand had ever been a baptism at all. It was dated. The whole body that kept it remembered it, and not one man's memory alone. That is the day we can show you.

cite.text:
Three things, and we will give them to you in the order that hurts.

The first is that we never settled our own rule against ourselves. We said, for a century, without qualification, that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing and must be given again. Then three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial - and afterwards took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. One of our own bishops came with soldiers to see it done. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two acts fit together. We were not hiding it: the exception sits in the surviving record of our councils, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We seem to have been able to hold both without feeling we owed anyone a reconciliation of them. That is the hardest true thing about us, and we would rather say it plainly than have someone else say it for us.

The second is that our founding generation could not answer its own question. At Cirta, before any of this hardened, our bishops were asked outright whether they had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned it on the man presiding. The room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would make a bishop's purity the test of whether a sacrament exists at all found that test unusable on themselves in that room.

The third we can show you in our own handwriting, because a court read it out. When a charge came against one of our bishops, another wrote urging him to settle it quietly before the flame burst out. He added, in the same letter, that he knew the accusation was true. Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Several of those letters end the same way. Let no one learn of it.

And underneath all three: a man among us argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our bishop told him never to preach it again. He did not recant and he did not leave. It is reported that we cut him off, and we never took him back. His book outlived us in the hands of the church that beat us.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your people never settle?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text:
Three things, and we will give them to you in the order that hurts.

The first is that we never settled our own rule against ourselves. We said, for a century, without qualification, that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing and must be given again. Then three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial — and afterwards took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. One of our own bishops, Optatus Gildonianus, came with soldiers to see it done. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two acts fit together, and we were not hiding it: the exception sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We seem to have been able to hold both without feeling we owed anyone a reconciliation of them.

The second is that our founding generation could not answer its own question. At Cirta, before any of this hardened, our bishops were asked outright whether they had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned the question back on the man presiding. The room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would make a bishop's purity the test of whether a sacrament exists at all found that test unusable on themselves.

The third we can show you in our own handwriting, because a court read it out. When a charge came against one of our bishops, another wrote urging him to settle it quietly before the flame burst out — and added, in the same letter, that he knew the accusation was true. Several of those letters end the same way. Let no one learn of it.

And underneath all three: a man among us argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop told him never to preach it again. He did not recant and he did not leave. It is reported that we cut him off, and we never took him back. His book outlived us in the hands of the church that beat us.

cite.text:
The empire changed what the church was. That is our whole case, and we are the party that said so.

Catacombs first, because it is the wrong picture. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions in our own time did not send us into tunnels; they sent soldiers into our buildings in broad daylight, under orders, to enforce a single church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting and licence, people clubbed to death with their hands stretched out to the Lord and their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us.

Then Constantine. We petitioned him, in the first year, through his own governor - we asked him to take the matter up. He gave us a hearing at Rome and then a council at Arles, and both ruled against us, and we refused both. A council can rule, but a court convened, staffed and enforced by a power that has already decided which side is the church is not the church judging itself. Our own bishop is remembered putting it to the emperor's commissioners in one line: what has the Emperor to do with the Church? The only man who wrote that sentence down was one of our enemies, and he set it in a paragraph about our bishop's pride and his fits of temper. We would keep the sentence and drop the paragraph. He would say we are being selective. We would say he was there to make us look mad.

We will not pretend we were clean about this. Three times we used the same machinery we denied had standing: when we asked Constantine for judges, when we asked a later emperor for our confiscated basilicas back, and when we turned the imperial law against heretics onto our own breakaway party. We did not hide any of it. It sits in the same texts that state the doctrine at its hardest.

Our neighbours said we washed people twice, that our country members were violent wanderers, and that we were the party of a man rather than the church of Christ - and one of our own petitions, signed by our own bishops, gave them that phrase to use. And to outsiders, the strangest thing of all: two of every office in every town, two bishops, two altars, and not one point of doctrine between them.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Did Constantine corrupt the church? Did the empire change what you were?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text:
We do not answer that as a charge. It is our case, and we were the party that said yes.

Start where the picture is wrong. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions of our own years did not send us into tunnels. They sent soldiers into our buildings, under orders, to enforce one church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting, and people clubbed to death inside it with their eyes shut, and many buried within its walls. That is what persecution looked like for us. Soldiers came to our buildings.

Now the emperor. We petitioned him ourselves, in the first year, through his own governor. He gave us a hearing at Rome and then a council at Arles, and both ruled against us, and we refused both, because a court convened, staffed and enforced by a power that had already decided which side was the church was not the church judging itself. Our own bishop is remembered putting it to the emperor's commissioners in one short question: What has the Emperor to do with the Church? You should know that the only man who wrote that sentence down was one of our enemies, and he set it in a paragraph about our bishop's pride and his fits of temper. We keep the sentence and drop the paragraph. He would say we are being selective. We would say he was there to make us look mad.

And we will not pretend we were clean about this. Three times we used the same machinery we denied had standing: when we asked for judges at the start, when we asked a later emperor for our confiscated basilicas back, and when we turned the law against heretics onto our own breakaway party. We hid none of it. It sits in the same texts that state the doctrine at its hardest.

quiet.statement: Two women stand at the center of our own history. One, Lucilla, a wealthy woman of Carthage, is named directly: her grievance and her money are said to have made the rival consecration happen that gave us our first bishop. A second woman is said to have stirred up the schism inside our own schism, years later, but her name is not given, even by the one source that draws the comparison. Lucilla had wealth and influence. Neither woman's own words survive. Everything we know of either of them, we know through a man's pen, written to explain why something happened, not to let her speak for herself.

dates.display: primate of this communion from c. 313, succeeding Majorinus, until c. 347; exiled after the Macarian repression and dead in exile. Birth date unknown; the byname Magnus is the tradition's, not a title he is recorded claiming.

names.name: Donatus, our bishop at Carthage
Donatus the Great, Donatist bishop of Carthage (primate c. 313 - c. 347)

dates.display: bishop of Constantina, the renamed Cirta, from the 390s; author of the letters Augustine answered in three books around 400-403; one of the seven Donatist pleaders at the 411 Conference of Carthage and, with Emeritus, one of the two principal voices there

names.name: Petilian, our bishop at Constantina
Petilian of Constantina (Cirta), Donatist bishop (fl. c. 395-411 and after)

dates.display: born about 350 at Caesarea in Mauretania Caesariensis; trained in rhetoric and the liberal arts; drafted the sentence of the Council of Bagai in 394, which implies established authority by that date; at the height of his reputation at the 411 Conference; older and embittered at a further dialogue with Augustine at Caesarea itself in 418

names.name: Emeritus, our bishop at Caesarea
Emeritus of Caesarea in Mauretania (b. c. 350 at Caesarea, modern Cherchel; fl. 394-418)

dates.display: seized at Vegesela in Numidia during the Macarian repression and killed at a cliff called Novapetra; the Passio's own heading dates the commemoration to a day in late November without giving a year, and the 347-348 dating comes from the standard field literature

names.name: Marculus, blessed martyr
Marculus (d. c. 347/348, during the Macarian repression; subject of the Passio Marculi)

dates.display: active as a writer and preacher within this communion in the 370s and 380s; rebuked by Parmenian and, it is reported, condemned by a council around 380; the Liber Regularum written in the same period and never suppressed

names.name: Tyconius
Tyconius (fl. c. 370-390; author of the Liber Regularum; condemned c. 380)

who_speaks.text: Five figures carry the Donatist voice across its recorded life. Donatus gave the movement its name and left nothing of his own but one question, reported by the man who argued against him. Petilian is its fullest surviving voice. Augustine quoted him clause by clause to refute him, but at the Conference of Carthage he spoke in the open. Emeritus argued that same hearing for three days, and his words were taken down as he spoke them. His church remembers Marculus as a man shown, before he died, what a finished life looks like. Tyconius was told by his own bishop to stop preaching, and his book later shaped Augustine's reading of Scripture.

documented_stories.teaser: Bishops in Numidia ask each other who gave up the scriptures, and several say they did. When the question turns on the man in charge, they leave it to God.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The bishops who later ruled that a traditor could never serve once faced that same question about themselves. They agreed to leave it to God, and sat down.
documented_stories.telling:
Before the quarrel over Caecilian began, the bishops of Numidia met at Cirta to make a bishop of their own. The year is disputed, 305 or 307 or later. Optatus tells the story of that meeting in his books against us.

Secundus of Tigisis presided. He asked whether any of them had handed over the scriptures in the persecution. One by one, several said they had. It was the same charge we would soon bring against Felix, the bishop who made Caecilian.

Then Purpurius turned the question back on Secundus. He taunted him for being let go only after a long time among the soldiers. The room began to mutter that Secundus too had given up the sacred books to buy his release.

Secundus asked advice from his brother's son, called Secundus the Less, who told him to leave the whole affair to God. Secundus then asked the three bishops who had not been accused for their judgement. They were Victor of Garba, Felix of Rotarium and Nabor of Centurio. They said a case like this should be reserved to the Lord.

"Sit down, all," Secundus said. "Thanks be to God," the assembly answered, and sat. No one was found guilty, and no one was cleared.
documented_stories.title: Bishops Who Left the Question to God
documented_stories.when: 305 or 307 or later (the council's date is disputed)

documented_stories.teaser: A rich woman is told off for kissing a martyr's bone. Then a disputed vote ends with a rival bishop. The story of the rebuke comes only from the man who blames her.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A rich woman is rebuked for kissing a martyr's bone before communion. Years later the man who rebuked her becomes bishop of Carthage. A rival bishop is made against him.
documented_stories.telling:
She kept the bone of a martyr with her, and she kissed it before she took the cup at communion. Lucilla was a wealthy laywoman of Carthage, and the archdeacon Caecilian rebuked her for it. Optatus wrote against us about fifty years later. He adds that the dead man was not yet a recognized martyr, if he was one at all. She left, he says, full of anger.

Around then, persecution broke over Carthage, and the bishop, Mensurius, was summoned to the emperor's court. He left the church's gold and silver with elders he trusted. He gave an old woman a written list of it, to hand to whoever sat in the bishop's chair if he did not come home.

He did not come home. Botrus and Celestius had both expected the office, but Caecilian was elected instead. Optatus says the elders had kept back more of the treasure than they should have. In his telling, the elders, the two passed-over men and Lucilla now found a common cause.

At a crowded meeting in the basilica, Caecilian demanded that his accusers state their charge. Purpurius only mocked him. Let his head be well beaten in penance, he said. No proof was produced. Instead Majorinus, a member of Lucilla's household, was made bishop in Caecilian's place. It was done at her urging and through her bribes, Optatus writes.
documented_stories.title: A Rebuke Over a Martyr's Bone, and a Rival Bishop
documented_stories.when: 311 or 312 (the Carthage election and the rival consecration)

documented_stories.teaser: The emperor orders a trial of the bishop said to have given up the scriptures. Under threat of torture, a town official admits he added false lines to a letter.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The emperor orders an inquiry. Felix, who made Caecilian a bishop, is said to have given up the scriptures. A town councillor admits, under threat of torture, that he added false lines to a letter against him. The inquiry clears Felix.
documented_stories.telling:
At the center of the case lay a letter to Felix, the bishop of Aptungi who had made Caecilian bishop of Carthage. Our side said Felix had handed over the scriptures in the persecution. If that was true, he had no right to make anyone a bishop, and Caecilian's office was void from its first day. The letter's closing lines seemed to prove it.

The emperor Constantine ordered the charge looked into, and the proconsul Aelianus heard named witnesses on the record. Their words survive in the dossier of documents Optatus kept. The letter came from a magistrate, Caecilianus. He told the court he had never dictated its closing lines.

Then a town official named Ingentius was questioned. Under the threat of torture, he broke. He admitted that he had added to the letter himself, out of grief over Maurus, his guest. A counsel named Apronianus charged that he had travelled through Numidia and Mauritania as our party's agent. Ingentius denied that he had been to Numidia.

The proconsul ruled that nothing had been proved against Felix, and he cleared him.
documented_stories.title: A Forged Letter and the Bishop Who Was Cleared

documented_stories.teaser: A Roman official puts named witnesses under oath. Bishops' letters are read aloud. One admits the charge was true, and several beg that no one find out.
documented_stories.tellable_as: In 320 a Roman official hears a case against Silvanus, bishop of Cirta. A witness agrees that he was a betrayer, and letters from our own bishops beg that no one find out. The charge also names four hundred pieces of silver from Lucilla as the price of our rival bishop.
documented_stories.telling:
In 320 a Roman official named Zenophilus asked what had become of the church's money. The charge came from Nundinarius, a deacon whom his own bishop had demoted. Optatus, our opponent, kept the court record among his documents, because its findings tell against us.

The charge named Silvanus, bishop of Cirta, as a betrayer and a thief of the goods of the poor. It said the noble woman Lucilla had given four hundred pieces of silver. For that money, it said, the clergy had plotted to make Majorinus bishop, and the split came out of it.

Then letters were read aloud. Purpurius, a bishop, urged Silvanus to settle with the deacon quietly, before a flame broke out that could not be put out without spiritual bloodshed. In the same letter he said he knew the charges were true. A bishop named Fortis wrote that they should not go into a public court and be condemned by pagans. Several of the letters end the same way. Let no one know about it.

Then a witness named Victor was questioned. Had Silvanus handed anything over? He had, Victor said, but not in his presence. Victor said he had fought against making Silvanus bishop. Pressed to confess what he knew, he said it plainly. "He was a betrayer."
documented_stories.title: Four Hundred Pieces of Silver, and Letters Asking for Silence
documented_stories.when: 320 (the inquiry before Zenophilus); the money and consecration it investigates date to c. 305-312

documented_stories.teaser: In his church's own account, a bishop is flogged, shown a cup, a crown and a palm, and thrown from a cliff.
documented_stories.tellable_as: On the last night of his four days at Novapetra, after a day of fasting, Marculus is shown a cup, a crown and a palm. Before dawn he is thrown from a cliff. The tradition says his body came down gently, and a bright cloud showed the brethren where he lay.
documented_stories.telling:
We remember Marculus as a man who had already turned from worldly advancement and given his life to the church. Our account of his suffering, the Passio Marculi, names no author. It gives a day but no year.

When Macarius's persecution came into Numidia, ten of our bishops were sent to meet him, and Marculus was among them. He was seized at Vegesela, bound to columns and flogged. The account says he bore it without visible pain and praised God the whole time. Then he was paraded through several towns of Numidia and held four days at a cliff called Novapetra.

There, the account says, he fasted and was given a vision. A cup, a crown and a palm were shown to him together. Before dawn he was thrown from the cliff.

We hold that his body did not break in the fall. It came down gently, we say, as though something carried it. A bright cloud covered it, and flashes of light showed the brothers where he lay, so that they could take him for burial.
documented_stories.title: A Cup, a Crown and a Palm at Novapetra
documented_stories.when: 347-348 (the Macarian persecution; the text gives a day but no year)

documented_stories.teaser: Bishop Macrobius writes to the people of Carthage about Isaac and Maximianus. The proconsul had them sunk in the sea so that no one could honor them.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A bishop writes to the people of Carthage about two of their number, Isaac and Maximianus. The proconsul had them sunk in the sea so no one could honor them, and the sea gave them back.
documented_stories.telling:
Maximianus, a soldier of Christ in the letter's words, was chosen to face the Roman proconsul first. The night before, at a shared meal, the wine in his cup seemed to take the shape of a crown. It shone with the colors of blood and light. Our bishop Macrobius told the story in a letter to the people of Carthage. He took it as an omen of what the next day would ask.

Maximianus was beaten with leaded whips and then with rods. Isaac was flogged beside him. He called his floggers traditores, men who had handed over the scriptures, and told them to come and heal their madness of unity. Both men were sentenced to exile and shut in prison, and there Isaac died.

That night, Macrobius writes, Maximianus dreamed he fought the emperor's officials and then the emperor himself, and struck out his eye. Then a bright youth crowned him. The proconsul wanted neither man honored as a relic. He had both bodies weighted with jars of sand and thrown into the sea. By the letter's account, Maximianus was still alive.

The sea would not keep them. For six days, Macrobius says, the bodies were driven back toward the shore, until they came up whole to the people waiting. Macrobius closes by telling his readers that the two martyrs wait for them with arms stretched out from heaven. He urges the living to hurry after them.
documented_stories.title: A Bishop Writes About Two Men Sunk in the Sea

documented_stories.teaser: A writer argues from Scripture that the church spans the whole earth. His bishop tells him to stop. He neither recants nor leaves, and a council reportedly condemns him.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A man argues from Scripture that the church spreads across the whole world. His own bishop tells him never to preach it again. He neither gives in nor leaves.
documented_stories.telling:
Tyconius argued at length, with strong support from Scripture, that the Christians of Africa belonged to a church spread across the whole earth. Anyone who followed the case could see where it led. If he was right, the African churches still in communion with the rest had lost nothing by staying. Those who had left that communion, his own party among them, had broken away from something real.

Parmenian, our bishop at Carthage, saw where the argument pointed, and he did not follow it. Augustine, writing against us some twenty years later, tells what came next. Parmenian wrote to Tyconius and rebuked him for preaching that the church spread across the whole earth. He warned him never to dare do it again.

Tyconius did not take it back, and he did not leave. He went on arguing from inside the party that had told him to stop. It is reported, Augustine says, that a council of his own communion then condemned him. He never went over to the other side.
documented_stories.title: The Writer Who Argued the Church Reached the Whole Earth
documented_stories.when: around 380 (Parmenian's letter; the later condemnation is reported, not witnessed)

documented_stories.teaser: Three hundred and ten bishops condemn a breakaway group as shipwrecked men. Later their church takes two of its bishops back, and does not baptize or ordain them again.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemn a breakaway party. They say its people are shipwrecked men who cannot even find a grave. Later our party takes two of those bishops back. It repeats neither baptism nor ordination.
documented_stories.telling:
In 393 a deacon named Maximian was made rival primate at Cebarsussi, against Primian, our primate at Carthage. In miniature, it was the act our founders had once taken against Caecilian.

The answer came the next year at Bagai. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met there and condemned the followers of Maximian in the harshest terms they had. Augustine quotes the decree word for word in his books against us. It calls them shipwrecked men, dashed by the waves of truth onto the sharp rocks. Their bodies cover the shore, it says, and they cannot even find a grave.

Later our party took back two of those condemned bishops, Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuris. Neither was baptized again or ordained again. Optatus Gildonianus, one of our bishops, used soldiers to enforce their return.

These two had baptized while in schism. Augustine made this the center of his case against us. If their baptisms could stand on our own authority, he argued, then our rule did not hold even for us.
documented_stories.title: Condemned as Shipwrecked, Then Taken Back as They Were
documented_stories.when: 393 to 398 (the Cebarsussi rupture in 393, the Bagai council in 394, the return of two bishops afterward)

documented_stories.teaser: Bishops refuse the chairs a judge offers them. For three days they argue before a court bound by an order that already calls the other side Catholic.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Our bishops face the Catholic bishops before an imperial judge. They refuse the chairs he offers, because Christ stood before his own governor. For three days they argue that a court which has already been told which side is Catholic cannot be the one to find out.
documented_stories.telling:
The judge sat, and our bishops stood. Flavius Marcellinus offered them chairs, and said it weighed on him to sit while so many venerable men stood. Petilian thanked him and refused. We do not blush and we do not fear, he said. Christ himself stood before the governor, so how could we refuse to stand?

This was Carthage in the summer of 411. The emperor had ordered our whole quarrel settled at law, and imperial notaries took down what was said.

Emeritus of Caesarea carried our argument. He would not let the court touch the case itself until it had settled the day, the mandates and who was bringing the charge. When the other side claimed the name Catholic, Petilian answered that it meant nothing until the case was decided. Marcellinus agreed that the name belonged to whichever side the truth was found with. Then he said he was bound by the emperor's written order, which had already given them that name.

On the third day Augustine argued from the wheat and the weeds that the church holds good and bad together. Emeritus answered him verse for verse from the same books. He signed the notary's record of most of what he said. At times he added that he kept his right to appeal.

In the end Marcellinus ruled against us, though the acts we have break off before his sentence.
documented_stories.title: Standing Before a Judge Bound by the Emperor's Word

floor_note.text: Both churches confessed one faith in the Trinity and in Christ. They confessed Father, Son and Holy Spirit as one God. For most of a century their opponents called them schismatics, not heretics, because no one charged them with a different creed. From about 400 Augustine called them heretics, and only for their separation. The emperor's law of 405 placed them beside the Manichaeans. Even so, in 417 Augustine wrote that most of them held the same faith as his church. What divided the two churches was a narrower question. Could a bishop's conduct under persecution void what his hand later gave?

highlights.note: Latin for those who handed over the scriptures in the persecution. Donatists held that such a man could no longer baptize or ordain.
The senior bishop of a church. The Donatist primate sat at Carthage, and the rival church claimed the same seat for its own man.
A Roman official who judged court cases in a province. One cleared Felix of the charge. Another put Isaac and Maximianus on trial.
A written ruling from an emperor. In 411 the judge said that an earlier rescript had already given the name Catholic to the rival church.
The word means universal. Both churches claimed it as their title. The state granted it to the rival, and the Donatists called that side Caecilianists.
Both churches confessed one faith in the Trinity and in Christ. They split over which bishops were valid.
They followed Maximian, a deacon. He was made rival primate at Cebarsussi in 393. In 394, 310 bishops met at Bagai. They condemned him.

highlights.label: Diocletian's persecution
highlights.note: Diocletian and his fellow emperors hunted Christians in these years. Clergy had to hand over the scriptures and sacred vessels. These were to be destroyed.
The Vandals invaded Roman North Africa in 429 and took Carthage in 439. That ended the Roman power that had judged the Donatists and coerced them.
A hearing at Rome in 313. Constantine sent the Donatists' case there. It ruled against them, and they rejected it.
A meeting of bishops in 314. Constantine sent the African dispute there. It went against the Donatists, and they rejected it.
A court hearing in 411, held on the emperor's orders to end the quarrel. The judge Marcellinus ran it, and he ruled against the Donatists.
Primate at Carthage from about 313. Exiled about 347, he died in exile. The movement bears his name. Not one page of his survives.
A Donatist bishop of Constantina, which was the new name for Cirta. He spoke for his church in 411. His letters survive only inside Augustine's replies.
A Donatist writer of the 370s and 380s. His Book of Rules gives seven rules to read scripture by. A council reportedly condemned him about 380.
Catholic bishop of Hippo from 395 or 396 until 430. He wrote against the Donatists, and he argued with them at the hearing of 411.
A Catholic bishop of Milevis. In the 360s he wrote seven books against the Donatists, and later revised them. Most of their early story comes through him.
The imperial officer who judged the hearing of 411, a cleric of neither church. He was put to death in 413 on another charge.

highlights.label: Paul and Macarius
highlights.note: Paul and Macarius, who forced the Donatists into union with their rival in 347 and 348. At times they killed.
A Roman province of North Africa and the Donatist heartland. Its towns in these stories, such as Cirta and Bagai, lie in today's Algeria.
An old city of Numidia, now Constantine in Algeria. Bishops met there in a council. Its date is disputed: 305, 307 or later.
Town of the bishop Felix, who consecrated Caecilian. Its ruins, at Henchir es Souar, lie in today's Tunisia.
A town in Numidia where 310 bishops met in 394. Its ruins, at Ksar Baghai, lie in today's Algeria.
The town where Maximian was made rival primate in 393. Its site is unknown.
The cliff where, by his church's account, Marculus was held four days and thrown down. It is probably Henchir Encedda, in today's Algeria.
The place in Numidia where Marculus was seized. It is identified with Ksar el Kelb, in today's Algeria.

highlights.label: Constantine
highlights.note: Constantine, who became emperor in 306. He had the charge against Felix tried, and the trial ended in 314 or 315.
A Donatist bishop who used soldiers to bring the two condemned bishops back. He is not the same man as Optatus of Milevis.
The chief city of Roman Africa, where both rival churches had their bishop. Its ruins lie in today's Tunis, in Tunisia.

legacy.text: Tyconius wrote the Book of Rules. A council of his own party is reported to have condemned him, but the book lasted longer than that party. It passed to the rival church, and it shaped how Augustine read Scripture.

The contest between the two churches did not end in 439. It went on under Vandal and then Byzantine rule for about another century and a half. In the 590s Pope Gregory the Great wrote letters pressing for an inquiry into Donatist rebaptism still going on in Numidia. No line from the Donatists to any church a person could visit today has ever been shown.

read_first.note: The earliest full account of how the Donatist church began. A Catholic bishop who opposed them wrote it about fifty years after the events. Most of what survives of those first years reaches us through him.

source.citation: Optatus of Milevis, Against the Donatists (De schismate Donatistarum), trans. O.R. Vassall-Phillips (London: Longmans, Green & Co., 1917)

read_first.note: Three books that quote a Donatist bishop's letters clause by clause in order to refute them. They hold the fullest Donatist voice that survives, kept because it could be answered.

source.citation: Augustine of Hippo, Answer to the Letters of Petilian, the Donatist (Contra litteras Petiliani), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, vol. IV

read_first.note: The transcript of the 411 Conference of Carthage. Here the Donatist bishops argue their own case in their own recorded words, and no opponent chose what survived. The printed copy is badly damaged, so its exact wording is a careful reading of a hard text.

source.citation: J.-P. Migne (ed.), Patrologiae Cursus Completus, Series Latina, Tomus XI (Paris)

relations_summary.text: The Donatists denied that the state could judge the church. A neighboring tradition, Imperial and Juridical Christianity, took the opposite path. There, church office grew close to the power of the state from Constantine's time on. The same Constantine whom the Donatists asked for help in 313, and then refused as a judge, is where that tradition begins. Donatist rebaptism, given once for all, also stands against the Cappadocian answer to the same question. How does someone from the other side come back in? The Cappadocians let people back in by stages, with graded penance, as a tool of exact care and not as a wall.

sourcing.text: Nearly all the written evidence passed through two Catholic writers, Optatus of Milevis and Augustine of Hippo, before it reached us. That is the central problem with the sources. Four short texts speak as Donatists rather than about them. The transcript of the 411 hearing also keeps their bishops' own words, chosen by no opponent. The clearest exception is two words, Deo laudes, cut into stone. No report or plan of the Numidian churches where such words were spoken is among the sources. One more scholarly dispute runs through all the evidence. Was the hostile picture of the Circumcellions, rural members of the movement, true to them, or mainly their opponents' polemic?

story.text: From around 311, two rival churches stood side by side in Roman North Africa, centered on Carthage and Numidia. Both churches confessed one faith in the Trinity and in Christ. They split over whether a bishop's conduct under persecution could void what his hand later gave. One side said it could. It saw itself as the pure, persecuted church of the martyrs, the one true church. History calls its members Donatists, after an early bishop. Optatus, an opponent, says its bishops called themselves 'the party of Donatus' when questioned in court. Whether they used that name among themselves is not known.

The quarrel began in the persecution of 303 to 305. Officials demanded that clergy hand over the scriptures and the church's vessels to be destroyed. Some did. Others refused and suffered for it. The Donatists held that what a minister did in that moment decided whether his hand could be trusted afterward. In 311 or 312, Caecilian was elected bishop of Carthage. Felix of Aptungi, who ordained him, was accused of handing over the scriptures. If that was true, they held, the new bishop was no bishop at all. A rival party made Majorinus bishop in his place. The emperor later had the charge against Felix tried. Under threat of torture, a witness admitted forging part of the evidence, and Felix was cleared.

For a century, anyone who crossed over from the rival church was washed again. The Donatists did not count it as a second baptism. A hand from a broken line had given nothing the first time. Imperial edicts named the practice as an offense.

Persecution came again in 347 and 348. This time it came at the rival church's urging, through the emperor's commissioners. The Donatists' own account says that Bishop Marculus was held four days at a cliff called Novapetra. There he fasted and was shown a vision of a cup, a crown and a palm. Then he was thrown down. Two laymen of Carthage, Isaac and Maximianus, were flogged and sunk in the sea. Every year, at the grave, they read such accounts aloud.

By the later fourth century it was a full parallel church, with its own bishops, basilicas and councils in the same towns as its rival. In Numidia it far outnumbered the other church. There it was the ordinary church of the village.

Optatus also reports that their bishop Donatus once asked what the emperor had to do with the church. The hearing at Rome in 313 and the Council of Arles in 314 ruled against them, and they rejected both rulings. A council called and enforced by a state that already favored their rival was not, in their view, the church judging itself. Still, three times they turned to the state when that served their case. They petitioned Constantine in 313 and Julian in 361. In the 390s they invoked imperial law against their own breakaway Maximianists.

At the Conference of Carthage in 411, about two hundred and eighty Donatist bishops faced a slightly larger number of rivals. The imperial judge offered them chairs, and they refused. Christ had stood before his governor, said Petilian, one of their speakers, and so would they. The judge granted that the name Catholic belonged to whichever side held the truth. Then he said he was bound by an imperial rescript that had already given the name to the other side. He ruled against the Donatists, and penal laws followed.

This story ends in 439, when a Vandal army took Carthage. That removed the Roman power the Donatists had defined themselves against. The contest went on under the Vandals, and then under the emperors of the East. In the 590s Pope Gregory the Great wrote of rebaptism still going on in Numidia, and pressed for an inquiry.

Almost everything known about the Donatists was written by two men arguing against them. Most of their own words survive only as quotations in those men's books. Four short texts speak for them directly, and so do their bishops at the hearing of 411. So do two words cut into pillars near Bagai, Deo laudes, praise to God.

dates.display: primate of this communion from c. 313, succeeding Majorinus, until c. 347; exiled after the Macarian repression and dead in exile. Birth date unknown; the byname Magnus is the tradition's, not a title he is recorded claiming.

names.name: Donatus, our bishop at Carthage
Donatus the Great, Donatist bishop of Carthage (primate c. 313 - c. 347)

voices.hedge: Almost everything said of Donatus reaches us through an opponent who argued against him. One modern scholar guessed that Donatus himself preached the sermon read each year on the twelfth of March. He hedged the guess himself, and no source confirms it.
voices.text: Donatus followed Majorinus as bishop of Carthage around 313. He led his church for more than thirty years, and history names the whole movement after him. He left no writing of his own. His best-known words come from Optatus, the bishop who wrote against him. When the emperor's men came to Carthage with aid, Optatus says, Donatus asked what the emperor had to do with the church. He was sent into exile after the repression under Macarius, and he died there.

dates.display: bishop of Constantina, the renamed Cirta, from the 390s; author of the letters Augustine answered in three books around 400-403; one of the seven Donatist pleaders at the 411 Conference of Carthage and, with Emeritus, one of the two principal voices there

names.name: Petilian, our bishop at Constantina
Petilian of Constantina (Cirta), Donatist bishop (fl. c. 395-411 and after)

voices.hedge: His letters survive only in the clauses Augustine chose to quote and answer, and that choice favors what could be answered. At the 411 hearing no opponent chose his words. But the only printed copy read is badly damaged, so even his words there come from a careful reading of a difficult text.
voices.text: Petilian became bishop of Constantina, the new name for Cirta, in the 390s. More of his words survive than of any other Donatist, because Augustine quoted his letters clause by clause in three books to refute them. At the Conference of Carthage in 411 he spoke on an open transcript. He thanked the judge for the offer of a chair and refused it. Christ himself, he said, had not refused to stand before his governor.

dates.display: born about 350 at Caesarea in Mauretania Caesariensis; trained in rhetoric and the liberal arts; drafted the sentence of the Council of Bagai in 394, which implies established authority by that date; at the height of his reputation at the 411 Conference; older and embittered at a further dialogue with Augustine at Caesarea itself in 418

names.name: Emeritus, our bishop at Caesarea
Emeritus of Caesarea in Mauretania (b. c. 350 at Caesarea, modern Cherchel; fl. 394-418)

voices.hedge: The transcript survives in a badly damaged printed copy. Only about nineteen hundred of its 144,733 lines have been read, found by searching for his name. His later debate with Augustine in 418 is a separate work that has not been read.
voices.text: Emeritus, bishop of Caesarea in Mauretania, carried the Donatist case for three days at the Conference of Carthage in 411. An imperial notary took down his words as he spoke them. No other figure of his church is heard so directly. He would not let the court touch the case itself until it had settled the day, the mandates and who was bringing the charge. When the argument reached Scripture, he answered a reading of the wheat and the weeds verse for verse, from the same books. He signed the notary's record of most of what he said. At times he added that he kept his right to appeal.

dates.display: seized at Vegesela in Numidia during the Macarian repression and killed at a cliff called Novapetra; the Passio's own heading dates the commemoration to a day in late November without giving a year, and the 347-348 dating comes from the standard field literature

names.name: Marculus, blessed martyr
Marculus (d. c. 347/348, during the Macarian repression; subject of the Passio Marculi)

voices.hedge: Two hostile writers confirm his death, and each disputes its meaning in a different way. Optatus argues that the killing was a just punishment for schism. Augustine argues that the word martyr does not apply. The vision, the unbroken fall and the light over the place are his church's own testimony about what his death meant. No outside witness confirms them.
voices.text: Marculus is remembered as a man who had given up worldly advancement before the persecution found him. He was seized during the repression under Macarius, flogged, and paraded through several towns of Numidia. Then he was held four days at a cliff called Novapetra. His church's own account says he fasted there and was shown a vision of a cup, a crown and a palm. Before dawn he was thrown from the cliff.

dates.display: active as a writer and preacher within this communion in the 370s and 380s; rebuked by Parmenian and, it is reported, condemned by a council around 380; the Liber Regularum written in the same period and never suppressed

names.name: Tyconius
Tyconius (fl. c. 370-390; author of the Liber Regularum; condemned c. 380)

voices.hedge: His seven rules for reading Scripture survive complete. What is said of their content rests on a study from 1920, not on his own Latin. The condemnation carries Augustine's own hedge, it is reported. His formal standing in his church, before or after the rebuke, is left open.
voices.text: Tyconius was a Donatist writer and preacher, and the one Donatist thinker whose own book survives entire. He argued from Scripture that the church was spread across the whole earth. His own bishop at Carthage, Parmenian, told him never to preach it again. He did not take it back, and he did not go over to the other side. He went on arguing from inside the party that had told him to stop. It is reported that a council of his own church then condemned him.

tile.text: From around 311, in Roman North Africa, two churches stood in town after town, each with its own bishop, altar and line of ordination. The split began with a charge. The bishop who consecrated the new bishop of Carthage was said to have handed the scriptures over to be burned. If that hand was tainted, the Donatists held, all it gave afterward was empty. So they built a church of their own, with its own bishops. Anyone who came over to it was washed again by a hand that had never failed. It saw itself as the pure, persecuted church of the martyrs. Persecution came again, at the rival church's urging. The Donatists kept the names of their dead and read their stories aloud each year at the grave. They denied any emperor the right to say which church was true. Yet three times, when it served their case, they turned to the emperor's power. Nearly everything known of them comes from two bishops who wrote against them. Most of their own words survive as quotations in those books. Beyond those, they speak in four short texts, in their bishops' words at the hearing of 411, and in two words cut into stone.
